why_how.text: Points add up quickly, and knowing the values helps you see how close a record is to a required course or suspension.
A safety course can take points off, but a required course has a deadline that can cost you your privileges.

scenario.text: Raj, aged twenty-four, is convicted of driving twenty miles per hour over the limit and, nine months later, of tailgating.

reasoning.text: Sixteen to twenty-five over is listed at four points and tailgating at six, and two convictions within twelve months let the BMV require a safety course for a driver twenty-one or older.

result.text: If the BMV mails Raj a notice, he must finish an approved course within ninety days of the notice date or lose his privileges.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a court-ordered safety course always earns the four-point credit.

correction.text: The court chooses the type of course, but the four-point credit applies only when the course is BMV-approved.

memory_support.text: Two, four, six for speeding; points last two years; credit once in three.

prompt.text: A driver is convicted of going thirty miles per hour over the limit. Using the speeding bands, how many points is that?

answer.text: Six points, because twenty-six or more over is the six-point band.

rationale.text: The bands are two points for one to fifteen over, four for sixteen to twenty-five, and six for twenty-six or more.

lines.text: Courses can help or be required.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on points and the Driver Safety Program. Every traffic violation in Indiana carries a point value, and those points build up on your driver record. You will learn who sets the values, the speeding bands and other common examples, how long points stay active, how a BMV-approved safety course can earn you a credit, and when the BMV can require you to take a course, with a firm deadline that leads to a suspension if you miss it. Points are where many driving problems begin, so this lesson is worth knowing well.

lines.text: One to fifteen over: two points.
Sixteen to twenty-five over: four points.
Twenty-six or more over: six points.

narration.text: Indiana's Point Study Committee gives each traffic violation a point value that reflects how severe the violation is and its history. Speeding shows how the values climb. Driving one to fifteen miles per hour above the speed limit is listed as a two-point violation. Driving sixteen to twenty-five miles per hour above the limit is listed at four points. Driving twenty-six or more miles per hour above the limit is listed at six points. The bands are easy to mix up at the edges, so remember that four points ends at twenty-five over and six points starts at twenty-six over.

lines.text: Yield, tailgating six; suspended, racing eight.

narration.text: The manual lists other examples. Not using headlights and driving without brake or signal lights are each listed at two points. A hand-held device violation, an unsafe lane movement and ignoring a stop or yield sign are each listed at four points. Failing to yield to an emergency vehicle and tailgating are each listed at six points. Driving while suspended and taking part in a speed contest on the road are each listed at eight points. Whatever the value, points remain active on your Indiana driver record for two years counted from the date of conviction, not from the date of the ticket.

lines.text: Four-point credit, once per three years.
Processing takes seven to ten business days.

narration.text: A BMV-approved Driver Safety Program is a defensive driving course offered in classroom, online or DVD formats. Any Indiana driver who finishes a course from a BMV-approved provider earns a four-point credit, but only one such credit is allowed in any three-year period. If a court orders you to take a course, the court chooses the type, but the four-point credit is applied only for a BMV-approved course. Plan for some processing time too, because the BMV needs about seven to ten business days to process completion results before the credit appears.

lines.text: Twenty-one plus: two convictions in twelve months.

narration.text: The BMV may require a driver aged twenty-one or older who is convicted of two or more traffic offenses within twelve months to complete an approved course. Drivers under twenty-one can be required after two or more convictions, with no time window stated. A driver whom the BMV requires to take the course receives a mailed notice and must complete an approved course within ninety days of the notice date. Missing that deadline suspends driving privileges until the course is completed and the BMV has processed the completion. So a required course is not optional, and the clock starts on the notice date.

lines.text: Trap: any court course earns credit.
Trap: the credit can be repeated yearly.

narration.text: Here are two traps. First, a court-ordered course does not automatically earn the four-point credit. The court can choose the type of course, but only a BMV-approved course earns the credit. Second, the credit has a limit. You can earn only one four-point credit in any three-year period, which is a different number from the two years that points stay active. A related mix-up involves the ninety-day deadline. That is how long you have to finish a course the BMV requires, and missing it brings a suspension. Keep the two years, the three years and the ninety days separate.

Here is a quick check: a driver is convicted of going thirty miles per hour over the speed limit. Using the speeding bands, how many points is that violation listed at? Walk through the bands. One to fifteen over is two points, sixteen to twenty-five over is four points, and twenty-six or more over is six points. Thirty is more than twenty-six, so the answer is six points, and those points stay active for two years from the conviction date. If you chose four points, remember that the four-point band ends at twenty-five over.

Let us wrap up. The Point Study Committee sets point values by severity and history. Speeding is two points for one to fifteen over, four for sixteen to twenty-five, and six for twenty-six or more. Lights problems are two points, device, lane and sign violations four, emergency-vehicle yielding and tailgating six, and driving while suspended or racing eight. Points stay active for two years from conviction. An approved course earns a four-point credit once in three years, and a required course must be finished within ninety days of the notice, or privileges are suspended.

why_how.text: Driving without insurance is against Indiana law, and the minimum limits tell you what coverage you must carry.
When the BMV asks for proof, a fast response from your insurer prevents a suspension.

scenario.text: After a fender bender, Ana receives a BMV request to verify her insurance.

reasoning.text: An auto accident is a listed trigger, and her insurer must send a Certificate of Compliance that the BMV receives and processes within ninety days of the mailing.

result.text: Ana calls her insurer the same day, the certificate is filed electronically, and her privileges stay in place.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you can prove insurance by mailing the BMV a photo of your insurance card.

correction.text: Your insurer must send a Certificate of Compliance to the BMV electronically.

memory_support.text: Twenty-five, fifty, twenty-five; insurer files within ninety days.

prompt.text: Ana's insurer has not sent anything to the BMV ninety-five days after the request was mailed. What happens?

answer.text: Her driving privileges are suspended, because the certificate had to be processed within ninety days.

rationale.text: The Certificate of Compliance must be received and processed within ninety days of the BMV mailing its request.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on insurance requirements. In Indiana you may not drive unless financial responsibility, meaning insurance, is in effect. In this lesson you will learn the minimum coverage every driver must carry, the situations that lead the BMV to ask you to prove it, how your insurer proves it for you with a Certificate of Compliance, and the deadline that applies. You will also see what happens with company or rental cars and with court convictions for driving uninsured, and how a suspension from such a conviction is lifted.

lines.text: Fifty thousand for two or more; twenty-five thousand property.

narration.text: Indiana law bars anyone from driving a motor vehicle in the state unless financial responsibility is in effect for that vehicle or the driver is otherwise insured. The state minimum, commonly called twenty-five, fifty, twenty-five coverage, is twenty-five thousand dollars for injury or death of one person, fifty thousand dollars for injury or death of two or more people in one accident, and twenty-five thousand dollars for property damage in one accident. Those numbers are the floor. Any policy you carry must meet at least those limits to count as proof of financial responsibility.

Situations that can trigger a BMV request to verify insurance include an auto accident, a serious violation such as a misdemeanor or felony, and a pointable moving violation within one year of two other pointable moving violations. A driver suspended earlier for not proving insurance can be asked again after any later pointable moving violation. If the request comes, contact your insurer right away and have it send a Certificate of Compliance to the BMV electronically. The certificate must reach and be processed by the BMV within ninety days of the BMV mailing its request, or driving privileges are suspended.

lines.text: Company or rental car: employer or renter signs.

narration.text: When the vehicle was company-owned or rented, the employer or rental company completes the affidavit on State Form fifty-five four thirty-four to prove financial responsibility. Court convictions work differently from BMV requests. Anyone convicted by an Indiana or out-of-state court of driving uninsured must contact that court to learn whether showing proof of insurance can remove the conviction. A suspension from a court conviction for driving uninsured, or for not filing insurance with the BMV, is lifted only after the insurer electronically files an SR twenty-two showing future financial responsibility.

lines.text: Trap: a card photo is proof.
Insurer files electronically, within ninety days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think proving insurance means showing their insurance card. When the BMV asks, the proof it needs is a Certificate of Compliance sent electronically by your insurer, and it must be received and processed within ninety days of the BMV mailing its request. Waiting until the last week is risky, because the deadline is about processing, not just sending. A second trap: a court conviction for driving uninsured is handled with the court, not the BMV. Contact the court that convicted you to learn whether proof of insurance can remove it.

Here is a quick check: the BMV mailed Ana a request to verify insurance ninety-five days ago, and her insurer has not filed anything. What happens to her driving privileges? Recall the deadline. The insurer's Certificate of Compliance must reach and be processed by the BMV within ninety days of the BMV mailing its request, or privileges are suspended. Ninety-five days is past that window, so her privileges are suspended. The fix would have been to call her insurer right away when the request arrived. If you thought there was a grace period, review the ninety-day rule.

Let us wrap up. You may not drive in Indiana without financial responsibility in effect. The minimum is twenty-five thousand dollars for one person's injury or death, fifty thousand for two or more people, and twenty-five thousand for property damage. Accidents, serious violations and repeat pointable violations can trigger a request, and earlier no-proof suspensions can bring more. Your insurer sends a Certificate of Compliance electronically, processed within ninety days of the mailing. Employers and rental companies complete their own affidavit, court convictions go back to the court, and a conviction suspension is lifted by an SR twenty-two filing.

why_how.text: An SR twenty-two filing is the key that stays or ends many insurance suspensions.
Reinstatement fees rise with each no-insurance suspension, so knowing the alternative can save money.

scenario.text: Jon's no-insurance suspension took effect in twenty twenty-three, and his insurer files an SR twenty-two.

reasoning.text: A no-insurance suspension that took effect at the end of twenty twenty-one or later is indefinite; the SR twenty-two stays it, and keeping it continuously for one hundred eighty days ends it.

result.text: Jon keeps the SR twenty-two in force without a break for one hundred eighty days, which ends the suspension.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a stayed suspension is gone for good once the SR twenty-two is filed.

correction.text: If an SR twenty-six cancellation arrives during the one-hundred-eighty-day stay, the stay is removed, the suspension is active again and stayed fees come due.

memory_support.text: File it, keep it, one hundred eighty days unbroken.

prompt.text: Mo has an SR twenty-two requirement, and his insurer sends the BMV an SR twenty-six. What does the BMV do?

answer.text: It suspends his driving privileges until a new SR twenty-two is on file or the requirement period ends.

rationale.text: An SR twenty-six is a cancellation notice, and while an SR twenty-two is required the BMV must suspend until a new one is filed.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on insurance filings and reinstatement. Once a suspension happens, getting your privileges back follows set rules. You will learn what an SR twenty-two filing shows, how indefinite no-insurance suspensions are stayed and ended, what an SR twenty-six cancellation does, the reinstatement fees and how to avoid them, how fees can be paid, and how suspensions for missing court or unpaid tickets work. Finally, you will see why driving while suspended is treated as a serious violation. These rules reward drivers who keep their coverage steady.

lines.text: Indefinite suspensions are stayed by it.

narration.text: An SR twenty-two shows that a policy meets the state minimums, and the policy cannot be canceled unless the BMV is notified first. A no-insurance suspension that took effect on or after the last day of twenty twenty-one is indefinite. An SR twenty-two stays it, and keeping the SR twenty-two continuously for one hundred eighty days ends it. If the insurer sends an SR twenty-six cancellation notice while an SR twenty-two is required, the BMV suspends privileges until a new SR twenty-two is on file or the requirement period ends. An SR twenty-six during the stay removes the stay and makes stayed fees due again.

lines.text: After twenty fifteen: two-fifty, five hundred, one thousand.
SR twenty-two can replace the fee.

narration.text: For no-insurance suspensions after January first, twenty fifteen, reinstatement fees are two hundred fifty dollars for the first, five hundred dollars for the second, and one thousand dollars for the third or any later suspension. Older suspensions dated before that carry lower fees of one hundred fifty, two hundred twenty-five and three hundred dollars. A driver can skip the no-insurance reinstatement fee by having the insurer file an SR twenty-two electronically and keeping it in force without a break for one hundred eighty days. Fees can be paid on myBMV.com, by phone, at a BMV Connect kiosk, or by mail with the BMV's coupon.

lines.text: Missed court or unpaid ticket: suspension.
Appear or pay to close it.

narration.text: Not appearing in court on a citation, or not paying a ticket after judgment, can lead to a suspension that the court tells the BMV to close once you appear or pay. That kind of suspension can be stayed by keeping an SR twenty-two on file for as long as the suspension lasts. Whatever the reason for a suspension, do not drive during it. Driving while suspended is a serious violation, and doing it with a prior offense can produce a misdemeanor or felony conviction on your record. The quickest way back is to fix the cause, whether that is a court date, a fine or a filing.

Here is the trap. Drivers sometimes treat a stayed suspension as finished the moment the SR twenty-two is filed. A stay only holds off an indefinite no-insurance suspension. It ends only after the SR twenty-two has been kept continuously for one hundred eighty days. If the insurer sends an SR twenty-six cancellation during that period, the stay is removed, the suspension becomes active again and any stayed fees come due. The same continuous coverage is what lets you skip the reinstatement fee. Think of the one hundred eighty days as a clock that must run without a single break.

Here is a quick check: Mo is required to carry an SR twenty-two, and his insurer sends the BMV an SR twenty-six cancellation notice. What does the BMV do? Recall what each form means. The SR twenty-two shows a policy meeting the minimums, and the SR twenty-six is the notice that it has been canceled. While an SR twenty-two is required, the BMV suspends driving privileges until a new SR twenty-two is on file or the requirement period ends. So Mo's privileges are suspended. If you thought nothing happens, remember why the policy cannot be canceled without notice.

lines.text: SR twenty-two stays and ends suspensions.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. An SR twenty-two proves a policy meets the minimums and cannot be canceled without notifying the BMV. Indefinite no-insurance suspensions are stayed by an SR twenty-two and end after one hundred eighty days of continuous coverage, while an SR twenty-six brings the suspension back. Fees after twenty fifteen are two hundred fifty, five hundred and one thousand dollars, older ones are lower, and a continuous SR twenty-two can replace the fee. Missed court or unpaid tickets can suspend you until you appear or pay, and driving while suspended with a prior offense can become a crime.

why_how.text: Alcohol and chemical test rules carry some of the longest suspensions a new driver can face.
Suspensions can also come from boating, child support and bad payments, and checking your record shows what you owe.

scenario.text: A driver with no prior intoxicated-driving conviction is asked to take a chemical test and refuses.

reasoning.text: Failing the test means one hundred eighty days, but refusing means one year, and two years with a prior conviction.

result.text: Because the driver refused, the suspension is one year, longer than if the test had been taken and failed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking refusing a chemical test avoids a suspension.

correction.text: Refusing brings a one-year suspension, which is longer than the one hundred eighty days for failing.

memory_support.text: Fail one-eighty days, refuse one year, refuse again two years.

prompt.text: A driver with a prior intoxicated-driving conviction refuses a chemical test. How long is the suspension?

rationale.text: Refusing with a prior intoxicated-driving conviction brings a two-year suspension.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on impaired driving and other suspensions. Alcohol is behind some of the most serious penalties in Indiana driving law. You will learn the legal limit and what affects a person's blood alcohol, the suspensions for failing or refusing a chemical test, ignition interlock devices, and what can happen to teens. Then you will see suspensions that have nothing to do with driving a car, from boating and child support to bad payments, and finally how to check your own record and track what you need for reinstatement.

lines.text: Intoxicated or over point zero eight: a crime.
Amount, speed and body weight set BAC.

narration.text: Driving while intoxicated, or with a blood alcohol concentration above the legal limit of point zero eight, is a criminal offense. Blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, is not the same for everyone who drinks the same amount. The main factors that set a person's BAC are how much alcohol was drunk, how fast it was drunk, and the person's body weight. So two people at the same party can reach very different levels. The safest plan is not to drive after drinking at all, because you cannot reliably judge your own BAC from how you feel.

lines.text: Refuse: one year, or two with a prior.

narration.text: A driver who fails a chemical test faces a one-hundred-eighty-day suspension. Refusing the test brings a one-year suspension, and refusing with a prior intoxicated-driving conviction brings a two-year suspension. After an intoxicated-driving conviction, a court may require an ignition interlock device, which checks the driver's blood alcohol before the car will start. Young drivers face an added step. When a driver under eighteen is cited for intoxicated driving, the Juvenile Court may also recommend a suspension. Refusing a test is never the easy way out; it carries the longer suspension.

An intoxicated-watercraft conviction is sent to the BMV, goes on the driver record and carries the same driving-privilege penalties as one in a motor vehicle. Reckless watercraft operation that endangers others, or running a boat while your privileges are suspended, is also added to the driver record. A court that finds a parent behind on child support may have the BMV suspend that parent's privileges at once until the court orders reinstatement, and a local child support enforcement agency can order a suspension that lasts until the parent pays or sets up a payment plan. Paying the BMV with funds that are not honored leads to an indefinite suspension until everything owed is paid.

lines.text: Official record is purchased and printable.

narration.text: Your driver record can be viewed free at any time on myBMV.com once you set up an account. That free Viewable Driver Record cannot be printed and is not official, while the Official Driver Record costs four dollars and can be printed for up to thirty days after purchase. The Reinstatement Requirements box near the top of a driver record lists any outstanding requirements and the date you become eligible for reinstatement. After a court's requirements are met, the court sends reinstatement information to the BMV, which may need up to ten business days to process it.

Here is the trap. Some people believe that refusing a chemical test is a way to avoid trouble because there is no test result. In Indiana the opposite is true. Failing a chemical test brings a one-hundred-eighty-day suspension, while refusing brings a one-year suspension, and refusing with a prior intoxicated-driving conviction brings two years. A related trap is the record. The free viewable record you see online is useful, but it cannot be printed and is not the official record that courts and employers rely on. Know which penalty is longer and which record is official.

Here is a quick check: a driver with a prior conviction for intoxicated driving is asked to take a chemical test and refuses. How long is the suspension? Recall the three penalties. Failing a chemical test brings one hundred eighty days, refusing brings one year, and refusing with a prior intoxicated-driving conviction brings two years. This driver has a prior conviction and refused, so the answer is two years. A court may also require an ignition interlock device after a conviction. If you chose one year, remember that a prior conviction doubles the refusal suspension.

lines.text: Point zero eight is the limit.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Driving intoxicated or above the point zero eight limit is a crime, and BAC depends on how much and how fast you drink and your body weight. Failing a chemical test means one hundred eighty days, refusing means one year, and refusing with a prior conviction means two years, and courts may add an interlock. Teens may also face a Juvenile Court recommendation. Intoxicated or reckless boating, child support debts and bad payments can all suspend your privileges. View your record free online, buy the official copy if you need it, and use the Reinstatement Requirements box to see what remains.

why_how.text: Repeated serious offenses can make a driver a habitual traffic violator, with suspensions measured in years.
Court-granted privileges let some drivers keep driving, but only under strict conditions.

scenario.text: Lou has nine speeding tickets and one reckless driving conviction within ten years.

reasoning.text: Ten or more violations in ten years with at least one major offense make a Section C habitual violator.

result.text: Lou is a habitual traffic violator under Section C and faces a five-year suspension.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking speeding tickets alone, however many, can never make someone a habitual violator.

correction.text: Under Section C, ten or more violations in ten years with at least one major offense, such as nine speeding tickets plus one reckless driving conviction, bring a five-year suspension.

memory_support.text: Two harms, three majors, ten tickets with one major.

prompt.text: Within ten years a driver has two judgments for offenses causing injury, neither involving alcohol. What suspension applies?

answer.text: A ten-year suspension as a habitual traffic violator.

rationale.text: Two injury-or-death judgments in ten years mean ten years; only two intoxicated or point-zero-eight driving deaths mean life.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on habitual traffic violators. Indiana sets especially serious penalties for drivers who repeatedly commit traffic offenses over a ten-year period. In this lesson you will learn the three tiers that can make someone a habitual traffic violator, the suspension that comes with each, and a worked example from the manual. You will also learn about Restriction five, which marks court-granted driving privileges, and the conditions a person with specialized privileges must meet every time they drive. These rules show how one offense can build on another.

lines.text: Two judgments in ten years: ten-year suspension.
Both intoxicated or point zero eight deaths: life.

narration.text: A person who, within ten years, collects two judgments for offenses causing injury or death becomes a habitual traffic violator with a ten-year suspension. Examples of such offenses include reckless homicide and failing to stop after a crash that caused injury. The penalty becomes even heavier in one situation. When both judgments are for intoxicated driving, or driving at point zero eight or more, that caused death, the suspension is for life. So this first tier depends on the harm caused, and alcohol-related deaths move the suspension from ten years to the rest of the driver's life.

lines.text: Section B: three major judgments, ten years.
Section C: ten violations with a major, five years.

narration.text: Under Section B, three judgments within ten years from the listed major offenses, including intoxicated driving or a BAC of point zero eight or more, bring a ten-year suspension. Section B offenses also include reckless driving, drag racing or a speed contest, leaving the scene of an accident, resisting law enforcement and any felony involving a motor vehicle. Under Section C, a driver with ten or more traffic violations in ten years, at least one of them a major offense, faces a five-year suspension. Operating a vehicle without ever having obtained a driver's license is one of the offenses that can complete the Section C count.

lines.text: Keep an SR twenty-two and the court order.

narration.text: A court-granted hardship, probationary, conditional or specialized driving privilege places Restriction five on the person's license. Anyone with court-granted specialized driving privileges must keep an SR twenty-two on file for the whole period, keep the court order with them or in the vehicle, show it to police on request, and carry a valid credential. One older code has been retired. Restriction two is no longer added to records for habitual violator suspensions or habitual violator probationary licenses expiring on or after January first, twenty fifteen. Specialized privileges are a narrow path, not a return to normal driving.

lines.text: Trap: speeding alone is never serious.
Ten violations with one major: five years.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers assume that speeding tickets, however many, can only add points and never lead to habitual violator status. Section C shows otherwise. Ten or more traffic violations in ten years, at least one of them a major offense, bring a five-year suspension. The manual's example is a person with nine speeding tickets and one reckless driving conviction. A second trap is the number of judgments. Two injury-or-death judgments start the first tier, while Section B counts three major-offense judgments. Count carefully, and check whether a major offense is in the mix.

lines.text: Two injury judgments in ten years.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: within ten years a driver collects two judgments for offenses that caused injury, and neither involved alcohol. What suspension applies? Two judgments for offenses causing injury or death within ten years make a habitual traffic violator with a ten-year suspension. The life suspension applies only when both judgments are for intoxicated or point zero eight driving that caused death. Neither condition for life is met here, so the answer is a ten-year suspension. If you chose life, check whether both offenses were alcohol-related deaths.

lines.text: Two harms: ten years, or life.
Ten violations with a major: five years.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Two judgments for offenses causing injury or death within ten years bring a ten-year suspension, or a life suspension when both are intoxicated or point zero eight driving deaths. Three major-offense judgments in ten years, such as intoxicated or reckless driving, racing, leaving the scene, resisting police or vehicle felonies, bring ten years. Ten violations in ten years with one major offense bring five years, as in nine speeding tickets plus one reckless driving conviction. Court-granted privileges add Restriction five and require an SR twenty-two, the court order and a valid credential.
